meta.title: Yukino — The AI coding agent that lives in your terminal
meta.description: Yukino is a terminal-based AI coding agent. Chat with any LLM, edit files, run commands, pursue persistent goals and orchestrate multi-agent teams — all from one CLI.

hero.badgeNote: — persistent goals, teams & keyless web search
hero.subtitle: Yukino connects to any LLM, edits files, runs commands, pursues persistent goals and orchestrates multi-agent teams — all from a single CLI that stays out of your way.

showcase.description: The same engine drives the terminal UI, a browser session over WebSocket, and a scriptable print mode for CI.
showcase.browserUser: Wire up the retry logic and show me the diff
showcase.browserQuestion: Wrapped the request in a 3-attempt exponential backoff. Approve to write it?

refactor.prompt: Refactor token verification into a single helper
refactor.thinking: Scanning the auth module and every call site…
refactor.answer: Moved verification into a single verifyToken() helper, updated 4 call sites, and all 12 tests pass.

ratelimit.prompt: Where is the rate limiter configured?
ratelimit.thinking: Locating the rate-limit middleware and its config…
ratelimit.answer: In src/middleware/rate-limit.ts — a sliding-window limiter backed by Redis, capped at 100 req/min per route.

darkmode.prompt: Add a persisted dark mode toggle to settings
darkmode.thinking: Reading the settings page and the theme provider…
darkmode.answer: Added a persisted dark mode toggle wired into the existing provider. Typecheck is clean.

audit.prompt: Audit the payments module in parallel
audit.thinking: Spawning two teammates in isolated worktrees…
audit.answer: Both auditors finished. 3 issues found — one critical (missing idempotency key). Full report attached.

goal.prompt: /goal Migrate the config loader to YAML, keep tests green
goal.thinking: Setting a persistent goal, then working it turn by turn…
goal.answer: Goal complete: the loader now parses YAML and all 14 tests pass — evidence attached, no further turns needed.

features.description: Yukino is built as a harness: a tight loop, a real toolbelt, and guardrails that you decide how tight to pull.
features.footnote: Built with TypeScript and React + Ink — MIT licensed.

multiProvider.title: Multi-provider by design
multiProvider.description: Anthropic, OpenAI, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. /login discovers available models automatically, keys resolve from the environment, /provider switches live and /thinking tunes reasoning depth from off to max.

terminalUi.title: A terminal UI that keeps up
terminalUi.description: Streaming text, thinking blocks and live tool output rendered with React + Ink — native scrollback instead of fullscreen capture, clipboard image pastes, ! and !! shell shortcuts, and steering messages that land mid-run.

toolbelt.title: A real toolbelt
toolbelt.description: Read, write and edit files, run Bash or PowerShell, glob and grep the tree, search the web without an API key, fetch pages as Markdown, query language servers via LSP, drive the desktop with ComputerUse and call MCP tools.

safety.title: Safety you can tune
safety.description: Four permission modes, two-tier allow/deny/ask rules, lifecycle hooks, and OS-level sandboxing via seatbelt on macOS and bwrap on Linux.

memory.title: Memory that compounds
memory.description: Memories are extracted in the background and recalled per turn, so Yukino remembers how your codebase works — layered with AGENTS.md instruction files from your home directory and every project folder. Consolidation currently runs in remote sessions.

sessions.title: Sessions & compaction
sessions.description: JSONL session logs resume exactly where you left off, while automatic compaction keeps long conversations inside the window.

skills.title: Skills & slash commands
skills.description: A skill catalog with hot-reload, inline and fork execution, plus user-defined slash commands loaded from two tiers — ~/.yukino/commands and .yukino/commands.

multiAgent.title: Multi-agent workflows
multiAgent.description: Spawn subagents, coordinate teams over file mailboxes, and isolate parallel work in git worktrees.

mcp.title: MCP, three ways
mcp.description: Eager, native deferred loading, or dispatch — chosen automatically so a fleet of MCP tools never blows up your context cache. Servers come from config.yaml and Claude Code-compatible .mcp.json, reconciled live by /mcp reload.

planMode.title: Plan before it writes
planMode.description: Plan mode locks the agent to read-only exploration. The plan lands in a file, and ExitPlanMode hands you an approval dialog before anything changes.

codeReview.title: Code review in the box
codeReview.description: /code-review audits your diff — workspace changes, a branch range, or a single commit — and returns actionable findings, no extra tooling and no leaving the session.

rewind.title: Rewind & checkpoints
rewind.description: Every turn snapshots the files it touched. /rewind rolls the conversation and the working tree back to any checkpoint.

background.title: Background tasks
background.description: Long-running shells keep going in the background and notify the agent when they finish — Ctrl+B moves them there, TaskOutput inspects and TaskStop cancels, so tests, builds and dev servers never block the loop.

hooks.title: Hooks on every event
hooks.description: Fire shell commands, prompts or HTTP calls on nine lifecycle events — session, turn, send/receive, tool use and shutdown — gated by JavaScript conditions that can even reject a tool call before it runs.

ide.title: IDE & browser companions
ide.description: @-mention files straight from VS Code, or run yukino --remote to drive the same agent from a browser over WebSocket.

observability.title: Observability, opt-in
observability.description: Export traces, metrics and logs over OTLP with OpenTelemetry, stream LLM observations to Langfuse, and report crashes to Sentry. Off by default, configured purely through environment variables — prompts, model output, tool arguments and file paths are never sent, and session IDs are hashed.

acp.title: ACP & A2A protocols
acp.description: yukino --acp speaks the Agent Client Protocol over stdio (--acp-ws over WebSocket) so editors like Zed drive sessions natively — while yukino --a2a serves Yukino itself as an Agent2Agent server that other agents can call.

library.title: Embed it as a library
library.description: Import @yukino.js/yukino to embed the agent, tool registry and conversation in your own host process — a terminal-independent entry for servers, editor extensions and test harnesses.

goals.title: Goals that persist
goals.description: Set an objective with /goal and Yukino keeps working turn after turn until it completes or hits a blocker — with token budgets, pause & resume, and state that survives compaction, /resume and checkpoint rewind.

webSearch.title: Web search, no API key
webSearch.description: The built-in WebSearch queries Bing's public pages directly — no keys, no subscription — while WebFetch reads any page as Markdown. Cancellable, result-capped and domain-filterable.

modes.description: The same agent loop powers every surface: an interactive TUI, a scriptable print mode, a browser session, headless teammates, native editor integration and an Agent2Agent server.

tui.description: The default experience: streaming chat, tool previews, permission dialogs, slash commands, ! shell shortcuts and keyboard-driven everything in a React + Ink terminal UI.

print.description: Non-interactive one-shots for scripts and CI — plain text or stream-json events, proper exit codes, and even persistent goals. It bypasses permission prompts, so run it only on trusted prompts.

remote.description: Serves the agent over HTTP + WebSocket and streams it to a browser UI — same session, same tools, any device on your network. Loopback by default; bind 0.0.0.0 to expose it (no built-in authentication).

teammate.description: Runs one headless team member per process. A lead agent spawns teammates in-process, or in tmux / iTerm2 panes when those terminals are detected; they coordinate through file mailboxes and a shared task board.

acp.description: Speaks the Agent Client Protocol over stdio or WebSocket, so editors like Zed can drive sessions, tool calls and permissions natively.

a2a.description: yukino --a2a serves Yukino as an Agent2Agent server — agent card, streaming status updates and permission hand-offs — so other agents and orchestrators can delegate work to it. Loopback only.

workflow.description: No new mental model to learn. Describe the task, review what matters, and keep a rewind button for everything else.

connect.title: Connect a provider
connect.description: Run /login or drop a config.yaml. Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible endpoints all work out of the box.

describe.title: Describe the task
describe.description: Ask in plain language. Yukino plans, streams its reasoning and reaches for the right tools on its own.

approve.title: Approve the risky bits
approve.description: Every write and command surfaces as a reviewable prompt — with allow-always rules when you want them out of the way.

ship.title: Ship and rewind
ship.description: Snapshots and checkpoints let you undo a turn, or hand the work to a teammate agent.

workflow.interruptBody: Keep typing while it works — messages steer the current run or queue as follow-up turns. Ctrl+C clears the prompt or stops a stream, and checkpoints let you rewind a turn or hand the thread to a teammate.

shortcuts.ctrlC: Clear input or stop the stream
shortcuts.ctrlV: Paste a clipboard image (Alt+V on Windows)

tools.description: Read and write files, run shells, search the tree, fetch the web, spawn teammates and call MCP servers — each one permission-checked before it runs.
tools.slashDescription: Drive the session without leaving the prompt.

providers.description: One YAML file decides everything. Configure several providers and switch live with /provider — keys resolve from the environment, so nothing secret lands in git.

anthropic.note: Native tool use, thinking blocks and deferred tool loading.

openai.note: Function calling with streaming across the Responses API.

openaiCompat.note: Any OpenAI-compatible gateway, proxy or self-hosted endpoint.

default.detail: The safe baseline for everyday work.

acceptEdits.description: File edits are accepted, commands still ask.
acceptEdits.detail: Move fast on refactors you already trust.

acceptEdits.note: File edits flow through; commands still pause for approval.

plan.note: Explore and design first — approve the plan before anything changes.

bypassPermissions.note: For sandboxes, CI and disposable worktrees.

sandbox.title: OS-level sandbox
sandbox.body: Wrap Bash with seatbelt on macOS or bwrap on Linux — optional auto-approval, an optional network kill switch, and it fails closed in every run mode when the backend is unavailable.

rules.title: Two-tier allow / deny rules
rules.body: User + project rule files like Bash(git push*), plus path-aware approval: writes outside the working directory ask first. Deny always wins over ask and allow, in every permission mode.

worktree.title: Worktree isolation
worktree.body: Risky parallel work runs in its own git worktree, so your main tree stays clean.

safety.localNoteA: Sessions, memory & file history stay under
safety.localNoteB: Nothing leaves your machine but the model request

agents.description: Fork your own context, fire off background subagents, or coordinate a full team over file mailboxes — with risky work isolated in its own git worktree.

generalPurpose.description: Researches complex questions, explores the codebase and runs multi-step tasks.

explore.description: Fast code exploration with parallel Glob, Grep and ReadFile calls.

install.description: Requires Node.js 20 or newer. The installer picks the latest release — with pinned-version and dist-tag options — and npm or pnpm work just as well.
install.ctaBody: Point it at your repository, describe what you want, and watch it plan, edit and verify — with you in control of every write.

faq.bodyA: Still curious? The full documentation lives in the repository and the CLI answers

providers.question: Which models and providers are supported?
providers.answer: Any provider that speaks the Anthropic or OpenAI protocol — Anthropic, OpenAI, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as a local gateway. Configure several in ~/.yukino/config.yaml, switch anytime with /provider, and /login discovers available models for you.

planMode.question: What is plan mode?
planMode.answer: A read-only mode for investigation and design — only its plan file is written. Enter it with /plan (Shift+Tab only cycles default → acceptEdits → bypassPermissions, and exits plan back to default): Yukino explores freely, and ExitPlanMode ends the mode with an approval dialog before implementation begins.

goal.question: What are persistent goals?
goal.answer: /goal sets a session-scoped objective that drives auto-continuation: after each turn, Yukino keeps working until the goal is complete or the same blocker repeats three times in a row. Goals support token budgets (--budget), pause and resume, survive compaction and /resume, and follow checkpoint rewind. After the 150-turn limit, /goal continue resets it — and the same loop runs in print, Remote, ACP and A2A modes.

sandbox.question: Do I need to run it in a sandbox?
sandbox.answer: No, but you can. Yukino ships with OS-level sandboxing: seatbelt on macOS and bwrap on Linux. Enable it in config.yaml (or toggle with /sandbox) and Bash runs isolated — with optional auto-approval, a network kill switch, and fail-closed behavior when the backend is unavailable. It applies to every run mode, and bypassPermissions does not disable it.

websearch.question: Does web search need an API key?
websearch.answer: No. The built-in WebSearch tool queries Bing's public search pages directly — no key, no subscription — and WebFetch reads any HTTP(S) page as Markdown. Both are cancellable and result-capped; WebSearch additionally supports allowed/blocked domain filters.

data.question: How does it handle my data?
data.answer: Everything is local. Sessions, file history and logs live under .yukino/ in your project, and memories under .yukino/ in the project or ~/.yukino/ in your home directory. Nothing is sent anywhere except your configured model provider.

headless.question: Can it run without a terminal?
headless.answer: Yes. Use print mode for scripts and CI (yukino -p "…" --output-format stream-json), run remote mode (yukino --remote) for a browser UI — --remote 0 lets the OS pick a free port — or expose Yukino to editors over ACP (--acp) and to other agents over A2A (--a2a).

ide.question: Does Yukino work inside my IDE?
ide.answer: Yes — in VS Code it connects to the Claude Code extension and turns editor @-mentions into file references in your prompt, with line ranges included. Any other editor works through the plain terminal, and ACP-compatible editors such as Zed can drive Yukino natively.

scrollback.question: Why doesn't Yukino take over my terminal?
scrollback.answer: Deliberate. Yukino renders on the terminal's primary screen — no alternate-screen takeover, no mouse capture — so completed messages land in your terminal's native scrollback, where selection, copying and wheel scrolling behave exactly as your terminal intends. Scrolling is controlled by the terminal itself; Ctrl+O reprints the transcript with tool output expanded or collapsed.

hooks.question: Can I hook into the agent lifecycle?
hooks.answer: Hooks in config.yaml fire on nine lifecycle events: session_start/end, turn_start/end, pre_send/post_receive, pre_tool_use/post_tool_use and shutdown. Actions run shell commands, inject prompts or call HTTP endpoints; conditions are JavaScript expressions, and a pre_tool_use hook can even reject a tool call before it runs.

teammates.question: What are teammate agents?
teammates.answer: A lead agent can spawn named teammates that work in parallel, exchanging messages through file mailboxes and a shared task board, with risky work isolated in git worktrees. Backends: in-process, tmux or iTerm2 — and coordinator mode narrows the leader to pure orchestration.

delegation.question: Forks, subagents, teammates — what's the difference?
delegation.answer: A fork (Agent without subagent_type) inherits your entire conversation and keeps nearly the full toolset — it's you, with full context. A defined subagent (explore, plan, general-purpose, or your own Markdown definition) starts fresh with a restricted toolbelt; pass run_in_background=true and it returns a task id immediately, delivering its result as a notification. Teammates are persistent named agents that outlive a single call and coordinate through mailboxes and a shared task board.

skills.question: What are skills?
skills.answer: Markdown playbooks that teach Yukino a workflow. The catalog loads from two tiers — user-global (~/.agents/skills/) and project-level (.agents/skills/) — hot-reloads when you edit them, and runs either inline or as a forked subagent. InstallSkill adds new ones from a local path or a raw SKILL.md URL.

memory.question: How does long-term memory work?
memory.answer: Yukino extracts memories in the background as each turn completes, stores them as Markdown under .yukino/, and recalls the relevant ones per turn — prefetched in parallel with the model call so nothing slows down. Consolidation merges and prunes them (currently in remote sessions), and /memory lets you inspect or edit everything by hand.

telemetry.question: Can I send traces to my observability stack?
telemetry.answer: Yes, and it's opt-in. Set OTEL_* variables to export traces, metrics and logs over OTLP (gRPC or HTTP), LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY + LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY to stream LLM observations to Langfuse, and SENTRY_DSN to report process errors to Sentry. Telemetry is off by default, and traces never carry prompts, model output, tool arguments or results, file paths or API keys — session IDs are hashed.

acp.question: What is ACP support?
acp.answer: Yukino speaks the Agent Client Protocol. Run yukino --acp for stdio or yukino --acp-ws [host:port] for WebSocket, and ACP-compatible editors such as Zed can create, load and resume sessions, stream tool-call updates and answer permission requests natively.

a2a.question: What is A2A mode?
a2a.answer: yukino --a2a serves Yukino as an Agent2Agent server: an agent card at /.well-known/agent-card.json, JSON-RPC at POST / and streaming status updates. Tool permission requests surface as input-required updates that other agents answer with a permission-response — and the server binds loopback only.
